From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Love, Anger, Madness [![Image 2: Cover of Love, Anger, Madness](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/0/0c/Love_Anger_Madness_cover_2009.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Love_Anger_Madness_cover_2009.jpg "Cover of Love, Anger, Madness")
Cover of the 2009 English translation
Author[Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet "Marie Vieux-Chauvet")
Original title _Amour, Colère et Folie_
Translator Rose-Myriam Réjouis, Val Vinokur
Language French
Publisher[Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard") (withdrawn)

[Maisonneuve et Larose](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maisonneuve_et_Larose&action=edit&redlink=1 "Maisonneuve et Larose (page does not exist)")([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maisonneuve_et_Larose "fr:Maisonneuve et Larose"))/Emina Soleil

[Modern Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Library "Modern Library")
Publication date 1968 (original)

2005 (reprint)
Published in English 2009
Awards Deschamps Prize (1986)
[ISBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISBN_(identifier) "ISBN (identifier)")[978-2-7068-1871-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-2-7068-1871-4 "Special:BookSources/978-2-7068-1871-4") (French edition, 2005)

[978-0-679-64351-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-679-64351-7 "Special:BookSources/978-0-679-64351-7") (English edition, 2009)

_**Love, Anger, Madness**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Amour, Colère et Folie_) is a 1968 collection of short novels published by the Haitian author [Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet "Marie Vieux-Chauvet"). There are three novels in the collection: _Love_, _Anger_, and _Madness_. _Love_ depicts a woman named Claire through her diary entries, _Anger_ tells the story of a family whose land is confiscated by a group of men in black uniforms, and _Madness_ follows a group of mad poets trapped in a shack by an invasion of "devils", a term they use to describe the local paramilitary forces.

Chauvet initially sent _Love_, _Anger_, and _Madness_ to French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") as three individual manuscripts. Beauvoir recommended their publication as a single volume to the publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard"), who published the collection in 1968. It was met with scorn from Haitian critics and, for unclear reasons, suppressed and withdrawn from circulation soon after its publication. After Chauvet's death in 1973, _Love, Anger, Madness_ was awarded the Deschamps Prize in 1986 and saw several new editions and translations, including an official French reprint in 2005[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-Frenched-2) and an English translation in 2009. Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted the book into a series of plays between 2007 and 2008.

_Love_ (French: _Amour_) is told from the perspective of Claire Clamont, a [mulatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto_Haitians "Mulatto Haitians") woman who lives with her sisters Annette and Félicia, as well as Félicia's husband, Jean Luze. Through her diary entries, Claire narrates her repressed desire for Jean Luze, who is himself developing an interest in Annette. Meanwhile, the local police chief, Commandant Calédu, terrorizes the local populace through home searches, [disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance"), murder, rape, and torture.

One evening, Claire watches through a keyhole in the door as Jean Luze and Annette are involved in what appears to be a sexual encounter. Later, Félicia, who is pregnant, faints upon seeing Annette and Jean Luze together, forcing Jean Luze to end the affair. After Félicia gives birth to a boy named Jean-Claude, a heartbroken Annette attempts suicide but survives and marries the scion of an influential [Afro-Haitian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Haitian "Afro-Haitian") family. The story then shifts to an extended flashback, with Claire describing her upbringing, the [colorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorism "Colorism") she faced as a child as the darkest-skinned sister, and the loss of her family's land.

Back in the present, Félicia becomes pregnant again, and Claire is tasked with taking care of Jean-Claude. As Félicia's pregnancy progresses, she falls ill, and Jean Luze takes her to [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince") alongside Claire and Jean-Claude to receive an abortion. Upon returning from Port-au-Prince, Claire, tired of repressing her desires, plots to kill Félicia with a dagger so that she can be with Jean Luze. However, as a riot breaks out targeting Calédu and his American allies, she instead stabs Calédu in the back.

_Anger_ (French: _Colère_) tells the story of the Normil family, whose land is seized by a group of men in black uniforms. The grandfather of the family is strongly opposed to relinquishing the land. The father vows to hold on to it, but his attempt to solicit assistance from a lawyer goes poorly. Rose, his daughter, is sexually harassed by one of the Blackshirts, who is visiting the lawyer's office, and the lawyer charges the family $500 upfront for his services. The father gets the money from his wealthy mistress, but the lawyer will not take it from him, insisting that Rose deliver it. Later, Rose's younger brother Paul sees her get into a car with the man from the lawyer's office, who is referred to as "the Gorilla". Realizing that Rose is having sex with the Gorilla, Paul vows to kill him.

The story then switches perspectives from [third-person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narration#third-person "Narration") to a series of [first person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_narrative "First-person narrative")[stream of consciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_of_consciousness "Stream of consciousness") narrations. A section narrated by Rose describes her sadistic [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape "Rape")[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-3) at the hand of the Gorilla. It is revealed that he told Rose that if she had sex with him regularly for a month, the family's plot would be restored. Meanwhile, the father sows division amongst the Blackshirts by selling the family's land in parcels, prompting the Blackshirts to argue over who gets what. In the ensuing conflict, one of the Gorilla's lieutenants shoots him. The grandfather is then killed by the Blackshirts alongside Rose and Paul's disabled brother. Rose dies from exhaustion soon afterward.

_Madness_ (French: _Folie_) is a stream of consciousness narrative told from the perspective of René, a poet hiding in a shack while a group of uniformed paramilitaries referred to as "devils" besiege the town around him. He is soon joined by another poet, André. After Jacques, another poet, joins them, René plots a rebellion against the devils using homemade [Molotov cocktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_cocktail "Molotov cocktail"). Their numbers grow again with the arrival of a fourth poet, a white man named Simon. Jacques, who is naturally timid, passes out from fright when Simon suggests opening the doors and eventually dies. After this, René, in a fit of madness, runs into the street and throws a Molotov cocktail.

After this, in an extended dramatic dialogue structured like a play, it is revealed that the poets have hallucinated the presence of the devils. The local police commandant arrests them for arson. Cécile, a woman living across the street, is accused of collaborating with them and arrested as well. The commandant interrogates the poets and orders their execution. René prays for aid from God, and the narrative ends with a vision of angels descending.

Publication history
-------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Publication history")]

[![Image 3: Woman with wavy dark hair and a button-up shirt with some puff to the sleeves](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)

An illustration of [Marie Vieux Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet "Marie Vieux Chauvet") by artist Claire Gaudriot

Haitian author [Marie Vieux-Chauvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet "Marie Vieux-Chauvet") began corresponding with French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") in 1967, asking Beauvoir to recommend her writing to French publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201530%E2%80%9331-4) She also described the oppressive conditions faced by writers under [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), whose dictatorship, beginning in 1957, saw an escalation of state violence deployed by the [Tonton Macoute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonton_Macoute "Tonton Macoute"), a paramilitary and secret police force.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201532Kim2016-5) In 1968, Chauvet wrote _Love, Anger, Madness_, her fourth book after _Fille d'Haiti_ (transl. 'Daughter of Haiti'), _La Danse sur le volcan_ (transl. 'Dance on the Volcano'), and _Fonds-des-nègres_ (transl. 'Negro Bottom').[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199358%E2%80%9359-6) She submitted the trilogy as three separate manuscripts to Beauvoir upon its completion, and Beauvoir recommended it to Éditions Gallimard for publication as a single volume.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-7)

### Initial release and controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Initial release and controversy")]

After its publication in 1968, _Love, Anger, Madness_ was met with public scorn from Haitian critics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-7) According to literary critic J. Michael Dash, the book's political boldness and its critique of the Haitian elite prevented it from achieving widespread acclaim.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998110-8) For unclear reasons, it was also withdrawn from circulation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231%E2%80%93235-9) Various accounts are given of these events. Writer [Madison Smartt Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Smartt_Bell "Madison Smartt Bell") claims that Chauvet herself convinced Éditions Gallimard to withdraw the book from publication.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmartt_Bell2011-10) According to [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy"), Pierre and his family suppressed its distribution by buying back unsold copies and forbidding translation, fearing government reprisal due to the trilogy's criticism of the Duvalier regime. Translator Rose-Myriam Réjouis claims the book's distribution was canceled due to concerns about the safety of Chauvet's family expressed by the Haitian ambassador to France. Academic Frank Laraque claims Editions Gallimard agreed to limit publicity for the book due to pressure from "spineless and cowardly people", hoping to protect the author's relatives who remained in Haiti.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012232%E2%80%93233-11) Discouraged by the suppression of _Amour, Colère et Folie_ and facing threats from the regime, Chauvet left her husband and Haiti in 1969 to move to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535Glover2016-12) She died of a brain tumor there on 19 June 1973.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012230Joseph201530-13) In 1986, she was posthumously awarded the Deschamps Prize, which is awarded annually to works written in French or a [French-based creole language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-based_creole_languages "French-based creole languages"), for _Love, Anger, Madness_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021Fondation_Lucienne_Deschamps-14)

### Posthumous editions and translations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Love,_Anger,_Madness&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Posthumous editions and translations")]

Several editions of _Love, Anger, Madness_ were published after Chauvet's death. An unauthorized edition based on scans of the 1968 edition was released by Voix de Femmes in 2003.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012238-15) Others were issued by [Maisonneuve et Larose](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maisonneuve_et_Larose&action=edit&redlink=1 "Maisonneuve et Larose (page does not exist)")([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maisonneuve_et_Larose "fr:Maisonneuve et Larose")) in collaboration with Emina Soleil in 2005,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-Frenched-2) by Zellige in 2008, and by [Zulma](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Zulma_(publisher)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Zulma (publisher) (page does not exist)")([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulma "fr:Zulma")) in 2015.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201513;_19-20Vitiello2021-16) German and Italian translations were released by [Ullstein Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ullstein_Verlag "Ullstein Verlag") and [Bompiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bompiani "Bompiani") respectively. A Serbian translation was released by [Laguna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_(publisher) "Laguna (publisher)") in 2008.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201520-17) In 2009, [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") released an English translation by Rose-Myriam Rejouis and Val Vinokur under its [Modern Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Library "Modern Library") imprint.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpear201520Vitiello2021-18)

Several scholars have analyzed Claire's feelings of inferiority in _Love_. Researchers Kaiama L. Glover and Keisha Simone Allan both tie these feelings to philosopher [Frantz Fanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frantz_Fanon "Frantz Fanon")'s concept of "[epidermalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Skin,_White_Masks "Black Skin, White Masks")", a term Fanon uses to denote the practice of associating black skin with inferiority and the difficulties this association imposes on black people.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318Hein%C3%A4maaJardine2021315Allan202395-19) According to Glover, Claire's sexual repression is the result of her mother's "ill-disguised shame at having a brown-skinned daughter" and therefore the "bigotry of the bourgeois mulatto community".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201319-20) Allan also argues that Claire's feelings of self-loathing are "linked to the racial tensions in her socio-political milieu".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllan202395-21) Both Glover and Allan tie Claire's personal struggle to the broader power inversion experienced by the mulatto community amidst the ascendancy of Caledu, who represents the [noirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noirism "Noirism")[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-23) state.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201319Allan202399-24) Allan also links her struggle to efforts by middle-class Haitians to distance themselves from their African ancestry.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllan202397-25)

Scholars have also discussed the ways in which portrayals of race and class intersect with gender in _Love_. Researcher Hellen Lee-Keller argues that Claire's narrative critiques the economic, political, and social structures that limit women's political and public engagement.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091293-26) She singles out the ways that the demands imposed on Claire due to her class and gender conflict with those placed on her by her family, leading to the "fragmentation of [her] identity.".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091297-27) Glover argues that Claire has internalized the hegemonic valuation of elite mulatto women's bodies as objects to be used in marital transactions, which contributes to her belief in her inferiority.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318%E2%80%9319-28) Researcher Kerstin Oloff Claire figuratively situates Claire within the [gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_fiction "Gothic fiction") tradition of the "female [zombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zombie "Zombie")" whose soul and agency have been stolen, rendering her a compliant, atomized figure trapped by the patriarchal and capitalist structures of her society.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOloff2018128%E2%80%93129-29)

_Love'_ s portrayal of peasants has also been the subject of scholarly analysis. Lee-Keller discusses the peasants that work Claire's father's land, highlighting the contrast between their impoverished existence and the Clamont family's obscene wealth, which is built upon their labor and the family's ignorance of their suffering in a reflection of [slavery in Saint-Domingue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Haiti "Slavery in Haiti").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee-Keller20091308-30) Oloff argues that Chauvet uses gothic conventions to link Claire's figurative "zombification" to the exploitation of the Haitian peasantry and the environment, with the zombie figure acting as a displaced representation of the socio-ecological alienation and material exploitation caused by United States imperialism in the global imagination.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOloff2018125%E2%80%93126,_130%E2%80%93132-31) Literary scholar [Colin Dayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dayan "Colin Dayan") observes that while Chauvet's peasants perform deference to Haitian elites, their apparent passivity is a survival strategy that masks subversive agency.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199895%E2%80%9396-32)

The classification of sexual violence in _Anger_ has been the subject of scholarly debate. Researcher Liddy Detar argues that Rose's sexual encounters with the Gorilla are best understood not as rapes, but as a form of political sexual torture, which systematically destroys the victim's language and world.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetar2002203%E2%80%93204-33) She further argues that Rose "develops an intimacy with the Gorille on whom her own life depends" to reclaim her agency and confront her complicity in the exchanges, subverting the victim/torturer binary and acknowledging mulattos' role in the historical exploitation of Afro-Haitians.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDetar2002210%E2%80%93211-34) Dayan compares the encounters between Rose and the Gorilla to the myth of Sister Rose, a mythical Haitian woman whose rape is said to have founded the nation.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199848,_122-35) She argues that Rose subverts this myth by "willingly offer[ing] herself in exchange for land".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan1998122-36) Researcher [Elizabeth Walcott-Hackshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Walcott-Hackshaw "Elizabeth Walcott-Hackshaw") characterizes this exchange as a "Faustian pact".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalcott-Hackshaw200545-37)

Chancy describes the encounters as rapes, emphasizing their brutality while simultaneously stating that they come as a result of a "poor choice" by Rose, who attempts to protect her class status rather than "undo[ing] the harms of the dictatorship".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChancy2004311-38) Researcher Régine Michelle Jean-Charles argues that what happens to Rose is rape because Rose submits her body "out of fear", which "obliterates the option of consent". Per Jean-Charles, Rose's rape is representative of the terror of the Duvalier regime, during which people's private lives "no longer belonged to them", and "is an example of how seizure by the state also extends to the female body".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles20067%E2%80%938-39) Researcher Laura Roldán-Sevillano concurs with Jean-Charles's assessment, describing the encounters as rapes and Rose as the Gorilla's "sex slave". She argues that while her family's fear and shame prevent them from helping her, she is empowered as a survivor through her own narrative voice presented at the end of the novel, challenging the culture of silence surrounding rape in Haiti.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTERold%C3%A1n-Sevillano202335%E2%80%9337-40)

Analyses of _Madness_ discuss its portrayal of the role of intellectuals under the Duvalier regime. Dash argues that the novel's portrayal of René, whose fantasies of liberation are ultimately self-serving and authoritarian, reveals the Haitian intellectual under Duvalier to be a tragically flawed figure who is alienated from society and who mirrors the oppressive culture they seek to resist.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998113%E2%80%93114-41) Literary scholar Raphael Dalleo argues that Dash's reading is reductive, countering that the novel takes a more "conflicted perspective" on Haitian intellectuals, mourning the exhaustion of a particular anticolonial modernist ideal while portraying the poets as victims of state terror—distinct from elements of the middle class collaborating with the authoritarian state.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalleo2011143%E2%80%93144-42)

Several scholars note _Madness'_ s use of the [carnivalesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivalesque "Carnivalesque") mode, first conceptualized by Russian literary scholar [Mikhail Bakhtin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Bakhtin "Mikhail Bakhtin") as a mode that uses popular humor to resist official hierarchies.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBirchHooper2012-43) Dash compares the structure of the novel to the structure of a carnival, describing the presence of the "devils" as a "gruesome masequerade". He concludes that the use of the carnivalesque mode in _Madness_ is a pessimistic illusion that reflects the "ludicrous nightmare" of Haitian society.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998116%E2%80%93117-44) Researcher Charlee M. Redman Bezilla argues that _Madness_ contains elements of the Romantic [grotesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grotesque "Grotesque") and carnivalesque modes, creating a chaotic public spectacle that lacks the "regenerative aspect" of the carnivalesque but that still opens a space for revolt and social critique.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTERedman_Bezilla201982-45)

The novel's use of religious themes is also noted by several scholars. Dayan highlights Chauvet's framing of [Haitian Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou"), not as a system of abstract beliefs, but as a form of inheritance that resists modernity's attempts to erase it.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199884-46) Meanwhile, Dash describes René's "esoteric spirituality" as a form of escape from the "psychic agony" he endures, comparing the poets to a "tiny, extremist sect". He also compares the poets' deployment of "images of martyrdom and apocalyptic rebirth" and their dreams of a "wrathful God, who with fire and brimstone will create order from the prevailing chaos" to the language used in the biblical [Book of Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation "Book of Revelation").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998115-47)

Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted _Love_, from _Love, Anger, Madness_, into a play in 2007. The play is an [abridged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abridgement "Abridgement") three-part monologue focusing on the character Claire.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019165%E2%80%93167-48) Adaptations of _Anger_ and _Madness_ were also produced and staged between 2007 and 2008 in [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,_Anger,_Madness#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-1)

15.title: Marie Vieux-Chauvet
15.content:
[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Marie Vieux-Chauvet |
| --- |
| [![Image 2: Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a3/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet_by_Anthony_Phelps.jpg "Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963") Vieux-Chauvet, Port-au-Prince 1963 |
| Born | Marie Vieux 16 September 1916 [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince"), [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Haiti_(1859-1957) "Republic of Haiti (1859-1957)") |
| Died | 19 June 1973 (aged 56) [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State "New York State"), U.S. |
| Pen name | Colibri |
| Occupation | [Writer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer "Writer") |
| Period | c. 1947–1973 |
| Genre | Novels, plays, short stories |

**Marie Vieux-Chauvet** (French pronunciation:[[maʁi vjø ʃovɛ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); born **Marie Vieux**; 16 September 1916 – 19 June 1973) was a Haitian novelist, playwright, and short story writer. Her novels are considered by translator [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy") to be "by far the best-known works by a Haitian woman novelist". Born in [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince"), Chauvet grew up during the [United States occupation of Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Haiti "United States occupation of Haiti"). She began writing at the age of 10 and attended the Annex of the Upper School for Teachers, receiving her certificate in 1933. During the late 1940s, she wrote several plays, and during the 1950s, she wrote her first three novels. She became involved with the literary collective Haïti Littéraire during the early 1960s.

Chauvet sparked controversy in 1968 with the publication of _[Amour, Colere et Folie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,\_Anger,\_Madness "Love, Anger, Madness")_ (transl. 'Love, Anger, Madness'), a collected trilogy of short novels. The book was met with disdain from Haitian critics and, for unclear reasons, suppressed and withdrawn from circulation. After the novel's suppression, facing threats from the regime of dictator [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), Chauvet went into exile in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where she died from a brain tumor. Her fifth book, _Les Rapaces_ (transl. 'Birds of Prey'), was published posthumously in 1986. Her work is noted by scholars such as Sophie Mariñez for its theatrical style, with common themes including gender, race, sexual violence, and [Haitian Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou"). She has served as an inspiration for other Haitian writers such as [Edwidge Danticat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwidge_Danticat "Edwidge Danticat") and [Ghislaine Charlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghislaine_Charlier&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghislaine Charlier (page does not exist)")([ht](https://ht.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghislaine_Charlier "ht:Ghislaine Charlier")).

Marie Vieux-Chauvet was born Marie Vieux in [Port-au-Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-au-Prince "Port-au-Prince") on 16 September 1916. Her father, Constant Vieux, was a Haitian ambassador and senator, and her mother, Delia Nones, was of Jewish [West Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") descent.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) Her early years were spent under the [United States occupation of Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Haiti "United States occupation of Haiti"), during which the United States instituted various socioeconomic and political reforms, including seizing land to create foreign-owned [plantations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation "Plantation") and re-instituting [forced labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor"), violently repressing resistance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt1995178Hallward200714Podur201213Glover2016-2) Her father, who was a member of the Haitian anti-occupation group Union Patriotique and editor of the anti-occupation periodical _Le Courier Haitien_, provided her with a political education.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016Jean-Louis202020,_142-3) She began writing at the age of 10, eventually attending the Annex of the Upper School for Teachers, an educational institute that trained [primary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_school "Primary school") instructors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231Glover2016-4) She earned her certificate in 1933.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) The occupation ended a year later, in 1934, with the withdrawal of American troops.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt1995xiii-5) At some point, she married physician Aymon Charlier. The couple had two daughters, Régine and Erma, before divorcing.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-6) She subsequently married travel agent Pierre Chauvet. The couple had one son, Pierre.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1)

During the 1940s, Chauvet wrote two plays. The first, _La Legende des fleurs_ (transl. 'The Flowers' Tale'), is an [allegory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory "Allegory") where flowers in a garden stand in as a metaphor for gender dynamics within society.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles201919Mari%C3%B1ez2020152-7) It was published under the pen-name "Colibri" (transl. 'Hummingbird') some time between 1947 and 1949.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-Legendedate-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199360Jean-Charles201915Mari%C3%B1ez2020152-8) Her second play, _Samba_, was unpublished but first staged in 1948.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMari%C3%B1ez2020152-10)

In 1954, Chauvet wrote the short story "Ti-Moune nan bois" (transl. 'Little Moune in the woods'), which was published in _Optique_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) She also published her first novel, _Fille d'Haiti_ (transl. 'Daughter of Haiti'), that same year. _Fille d'Haiti_, which won the 1954 Alliance Française Prize, tells the story of Lotus, the child of a [sex worker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_worker "Sex worker"), whose origins alienate her from her middle-class surroundings.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199358%E2%80%9359Vitiello2021-12) In 1957, she published her second novel, _La Danse sur le volcan_ (transl. 'Dance on the Volcano'), a [historical novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_fiction "Historical fiction") about a [mulatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto_Haitians "Mulatto Haitians") opera singer set during the [Haitian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Revolution "Haitian Revolution").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Glover2016-13) Her third novel, _Fonds-des-nègres_ (transl. 'Negro Bottom'), was published in 1960, winning the France-Antilles Prize for that year.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Vitiello2021-14) It explores the role of [Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou") in Haitian society through the eyes of Marie-Ange, a woman from Port-au-Prince who tries to help the impoverished inhabitants of a small village.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15)

Throughout the 1960s, Chauvet became involved with Haïti Littéraire, a loose collective of politically-oriented artists and poets who sought to broaden Haitian literature beyond its nationalist focus, advocating for a more human-centered approach to writing and promoting cultural and educational initiatives through a variety of artistic mediums.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1981203%E2%80%93204Kruidenier_Tolliver2012231Glover2016-16) Chauvet's exact relationship to the group is disputed. According to researcher Julie-Françoise Tolliver, Chauvet "belonged" to Haïti Littéraire.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231-6) However, according to researcher Kaiama L. Glover, she was only tangentially involved with the group during the early 1960s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) According to researcher Joëlle Vitiello, she hosted the group in her home on Sundays.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11)

### _Amour, Colère et Folie_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Vieux-Chauvet&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Amour, Colère et Folie")]

Chauvet began corresponding with French feminist [Simone de Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_de_Beauvoir "Simone de Beauvoir") in 1967, asking Beauvoir to recommend her writing to French publisher [Éditions Gallimard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Gallimard "Éditions Gallimard").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201530%E2%80%9331-17) She also described the oppressive conditions faced by writers under [François Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Duvalier "François Duvalier"), whose dictatorship began a decade earlier in 1957 and saw an escalation of state violence deployed by the [Tonton Macoute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonton_Macoute "Tonton Macoute"), a paramilitary and secret police force.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201532Kim2016-18) In 1968, Chauvet wrote _[Amour, Colere et Folie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love,\_Anger,\_Madness "Love, Anger, Madness")_ (transl. 'Love, Anger, Madness'), a collected trilogy of short novels.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359Glover2016-13)_Amour_ depicts a woman named Claire through her diary entries, _Colère_ tells the story of a family whose land is confiscated by a military commander,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) and _Folie_ follows a group of mad poets trapped in a shack by an invasion of "devils", a term used to describe local paramilitary forces.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998111%E2%80%93112Dize2022180-19) Chauvet submitted the trilogy to Beauvoir upon its completion, after which Beauvoir recommended it to Éditions Gallimard for publication.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1)

After its publication, _Amour, Colère et Folie_ was met with public scorn from Haitian critics and withdrawn from circulation.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012231%E2%80%93232-20) Various accounts are given of these events. Writer [Madison Smartt Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Smartt_Bell "Madison Smartt Bell") claims that Chauvet herself convinced Éditions Gallimard to withdraw the book from publication.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmartt_Bell2011-21) According to [Myriam J. A. Chancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myriam_J._A._Chancy "Myriam J. A. Chancy"), Pierre and his family suppressed its distribution by buying back unsold copies and forbidding translation, fearing government reprisal due to the trilogy's criticism of the Duvalier regime. Translator Rose-Myriam Réjouis claims the book's distribution was canceled due to concerns about the safety of Chauvet's family expressed by the Haitian ambassador to France. Academic Frank Laraque claims Editions Gallimard agreed to limit publicity for the book due to pressure from "spineless and cowardly people", hoping to protect the author's relatives who remained in Haiti.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012232%E2%80%93233-22)

Discouraged by the suppression of _Amour, Colère et Folie_ and facing threats from the regime, Chauvet left her husband and Haiti in 1969.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535Glover2016-23) While she had initially considered [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") as a candidate for immigration, she ultimately opted to move to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), moving from one apartment to another in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens") before settling in the [Upper East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_East_Side "Upper East Side").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535-24) In 1970, she married Ted Proudfoot, an American petroleum industry worker.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) In a letter dated 14 May 1971, she indicated that she was writing a book discussing her exile and relationship with Proudfoot.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012236-25) According to a subsequent letter dated 18 June 1971, she may have also moved to [Bronxville, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronxville,_New_York "Bronxville, New York").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJoseph201535-24) At some point during her exile, she completed the manuscript for _Les Rapaces_ (transl. 'Birds of Prey'), a novella told from the perspective of a young girl and a cat.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken201569Glover2016-26) However, she died on 19 June 1973 of a brain tumor before it could be released.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012230Joseph201530-27) It was published posthumously in 1986, over a decade after her death.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) She was working on two other books at the time of her death as well: _Les Fils d'Ogoun_ (transl. 'The Sons of Ogou') and _Le Cri_ (transl. 'The Cry').[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan1998119%E2%80%93120-28)

Writing and reception
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Vieux-Chauvet&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Writing and reception")]

[![Image 3: Woman with wavy dark hair and a button-up shirt with some puff to the sleeves](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg/250px-Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Vieux_Chauvet.jpg)

An illustration of Chauvet by artist Claire Gaudriot

Various sources discuss Chauvet's early dramatic work, particularly _La Légende des fleurs_. According to researcher Alessandra Benedicty-Kokken, the play analyzes societal notions of race, ultimately reflecting on the "tragically violent and humiliating consequences of Whiteness".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken2019222-29) Literary scholar Régine Michelle Jean-Charles gives an [ecofeminist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecofeminism "Ecofeminism") reading of the play, arguing that it uses its nature allegory to examine racial and gendered hierarchies. She describes the interconnected interactions of the flowers with each other and with the surrounding environment as representing an "ecological perspective", noting the uneven power dynamics between the flowers (which use feminine pronouns) and the sun, the butterfly, and the nightingale (which use masculine pronouns).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles201919%E2%80%9323-30) Researcher Sophie Mariñez posits that there is a "compelling case" that performance and theatricality, as exemplified in Chauvet's theatrical work, are defining elements of Chauvet's fiction as a whole.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMari%C3%B1ez2020152-10)

Glover identifies class, gender, race, and sexuality as common themes in Chauvet's first three novels.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) She argues that _Fille d'Haïti_ is a reflection of the political upheaval taking place in Haiti in 1946 under [Élie Lescot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lie_Lescot "Élie Lescot"), examining contemporary color-based tensions and foreshadowing François Duvalier's eventual rise to power.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover20137%E2%80%9321-31) Meanwhile, in discussing _La Danse sur le volcan_, researcher Curtis Small argues that Chauvet uses historical reconstruction to explore themes of gender and sexuality.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmall2009240;_242-32) Literary scholar Raphael Dalleo argues that the novel reflects Haitian [anticolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization "Decolonization") while also depicting the race, class, and gender-based tensions of the revolutionary struggle.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalleo2011129%E2%80%93130-33) Glover characterizes _Fonds-des-nègres_ as a critique of systemic corruption and gendered violence across Haitian society, while historian and literary critic Carrol F. Coates highlights its depiction of rural [Vodou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Vodou "Haitian Vodou") culture and the protagonist's transformative journey from alienation to spiritual belonging.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieux-ChauvetCoates1991564Glover2016-34)[Colin Dayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dayan "Colin Dayan") similarly notes the use of Vodou in the novel, discussing how Chauvet's portrayal diverges from typical idealized and academic representations, instead grounding the religion in the material realities of the Haitian poor.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDayan199882%E2%80%9383-35)

In _Amour, Colère et Folie_, researchers [Lizabeth Paravisini-Gebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizabeth_Paravisini-Gebert "Lizabeth Paravisini-Gebert") and Olga Torres-Seda identify themes of sexual and political repression.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParavisini-GebertTorres-Seda199359-15) Tolliver highlights the book's portrayal of violence against women, as well as its variety of narrative styles and its depictions of oppression, martyrdom, and resistance.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKruidenier_Tolliver2012229,_240%E2%80%93241-36) Glover and researcher Keisha Simone Allan discuss the character Claire's feelings of inferiority in _Amour_, linking them to [Frantz Fanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frantz_Fanon "Frantz Fanon")'s concept of "[epidermalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Skin,_White_Masks "Black Skin, White Masks")", a term Fanon uses to denote the practice of associating black skin with inferiority and the difficulties this association imposes on black people.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover201318Hein%C3%A4maaJardine2021315Allan202395-37) Jean-Charles discusses the deployment of sexual violence in the book, characterizing the rape of the character Rose in _Colère_ as being representative of social discourses surrounding [rape culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_culture "Rape culture").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJean-Charles200616-38) Analyses of _Folie_ discuss its portrayal of the role of intellectuals under the Duvalier regime. Dash argues that it portrays the novel's protagonists as tragically flawed figures trapped by their self-centered ideals while Dalleo argues that it offers a more conflicted perspective, mourning the exhaustion of an anticolonial ideal while distinguishing the protagonists from middle-class collaborators with the authoritarian regime.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDash1998113%E2%80%93114Dalleo2011143%E2%80%93144-39)

_Les Rapaces_, Chauvet's posthumously-published novella, is described by Glover as a reflection on the regime of [Jean-Claude Duvalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Duvalier "Jean-Claude Duvalier"), François's son.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlover2016-1) Meanwhile, Benedicty-Kokken describes _Les Rapaces_ as a formally experimental work that critiques totalitarianism, contemporary [biopolitics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopolitics "Biopolitics"), and the emergence of a [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") paradigm dominated by [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism"), the [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie"), and the United States.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenedicty-Kokken201557%E2%80%9358,_66%E2%80%9373-40)

According to Chancy, Chauvet's novels are "by far the best-known works by a Haitian woman novelist", inspiring other Haitian writers like [Ghislaine Charlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghislaine_Charlier&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghislaine Charlier (page does not exist)")([ht](https://ht.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghislaine_Charlier "ht:Ghislaine Charlier")).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChancy19978-41) Writer [Edwidge Danticat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwidge_Danticat "Edwidge Danticat") also cites her as an inspiration.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTETucker2019-42) In 1986, she was posthumously awarded the Deschamps Prize, which is awarded annually to works written in French or a [French-based creole language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-based_creole_languages "French-based creole languages"), for _Amour, Colère, et Folie_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021Fondation_Lucienne_Deschamps-43) Excerpts from her work were published in the 1989 anthology _Her True-true Name_ and the 1992 anthology _[Daughters of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daughters\_of\_Africa "Daughters of Africa")_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMordecaiWilson198984%E2%80%9389Busby1992271%E2%80%93275-44) Beninese playwright José Pliya adapted _Amour_, from _Amour, Colère, et Folie_, into a play in 2007. The play is an [abridged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abridgement "Abridgement") three-part monologue focusing on the character Claire.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019165%E2%80%93167-45) Adaptations of _Colère_ and _Folie_ were also produced and staged between 2007 and 2008 in [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) In 2016, on the [centennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial "Centennial") of Chauvet's birth, celebratory activities were organized in cities across the world, including New York City, Port-au-Prince, and [Montreal, Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal,_Quebec "Montreal, Quebec").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVitiello2021-11) As part of the centennial, a symposium on Chauvet was held, during which artist and academic [Gina Athena Ulysse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Athena_Ulysse "Gina Athena Ulysse") read excerpts from Chauvet's work; theater director [Alice Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Reagan "Alice Reagan") dramatized readings from _La Legende des fleurs_, _Les Rapaces_, and an unpublished draft of _Amour_; and scholar Lena Taub Robles translated Pliya's adaptation of _Amour_ into English.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Vieux-Chauvet#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaub_Robles2019180-46)
